source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are consistent with dehydration and concentrated urine, although urine specific gravity alone cannot establish the cause of the fluid deficit.","B":"The findings are most consistent with marked fluid overload because concentrated urine and dry mucous membranes usually occur with excess volume.","C":"The findings specifically diagnose diabetes insipidus because that disorder characteristically produces highly concentrated urine during water loss.","D":"The findings represent a normal hydration pattern that needs no further assessment because elevated urine specific gravity is expected in euvolemic adults."}}
source_row.rationale: An elevated urine specific gravity indicates relatively concentrated urine and can occur with body-water loss. Combined with thirst and dry mucous membranes, the finding is consistent with dehydration, but urine specific gravity alone does not establish the cause or a complete diagnosis. Diabetes insipidus characteristically produces dilute rather than highly concentrated urine.
source_row.source_detail: Clinical Information/Interpretation: increased urine specific gravity can occur with excessive body-water loss; decreased specific gravity can occur with diabetes insipidus. Interpret the result with clinical context rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis. Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog entry; live reference rechecked 2026-08-15. source_row.stem: A client has thirst, dry mucous membranes, and urine that is more concentrated than expected with an elevated urine specific gravity. Which interpretation best fits these findings?
